chunks.section: Train High, Ship Low: Efficient LoRA Synchronization for Distributed On-Policy Post-Training
chunks.text: Shenghui Li Affiliation: Uppsala University, Uppsala, Sweden Li Ju Affiliation: Uppsala University, Uppsala, Sweden Thiemo Voigt Affiliation: Uppsala University, Uppsala, Sweden Affiliation: Research Institutes of Sweden, Stockholm, Sweden {shenghui.li,thiemo.voigt}@angstrom.uu.se li.ju@it.uu.se

Transmitting LoRA adapters to rollout workers can bottleneck distributed on-policy post-training over bandwidth-constrained networks. Lowering the training rank may limit the capacity a workload needs, while adaptive optimizer updates are difficult to compress. Rollout workers can instead reconstruct updates from gradients by maintaining replicated optimizer states. We introduce HiLo , a compressor-agnostic framework that replaces parameter transmission with compressed gradient dissemination and local optimizer replay. By applying the same decoded gradients, the learner and workers maintain consistent policy states at the same version under reproducible execution. We further develop Spar , a budget-aware gradient compressor that combines spectral truncation, adaptive rank allocation and error feedback to decouple training rank from communication cost. Experiments across on-policy distillation and reward-guided post-training show that HiLo with Spar maintains learning quality close to full synchronization while transmitting as little as 1.6% of the adapter bytes, and accelerates end-to-end updates by up to 2.2 × 2.2\times under bandwidth constraints.

Post-training has become a key stage in improving the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Rafailov et al., 2023 ; DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ) . On-policy methods such as on-policy distillation (OPD) and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) learn from trajectories sampled from their own evolving policies, guided by teacher supervision or verifier rewards, respectively ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Shao et al., 2024 ) . The high cost of generating these trajectories motivates practical systems to parallelize rollout generation across many workers ( Sheng et al., 2025 ) . Recent systems such as INTELLECT-2 ( Prime Intellect Team et al., 2025 ) and ECHO-2 ( Song et al., 2026 ) disaggregate policy learning and rollout generation across geographically distributed resources, using Shardcast and pipelined broadcast, respectively, to disseminate policy weights from the learner to the workers over wide-area networks (WANs). Unlike off-policy distillation, on-policy post-training relies on fresh trajectories sampled from the evolving learner policy, so delayed synchronization can introduce rollout–learner mismatch and degrade learning ( Kang et al., 2026 ) .

Parameter-efficient fine-tuning, particularly Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) ( Hu et al., 2022 ) , reduces the synchronization payload to the adapter factors, whose size scales with the training rank. Synchronization can remain expensive over bandwidth-constrained WANs, especially when many workers share the learner’s uplink ( Song et al., 2026 ) . Although lowering the training rank reduces this cost, it also restricts the space of learnable weight updates. The rank needed for effective adaptation varies across workloads and adapted modules ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) , with very low ranks sufficient in some RL settings but inadequate for supervised fine-tuning or continued pretraining in others ( Biderman et al., 2024 ; Schulman and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025 ) . Ideally, the rank should be determined by the learning workload, while synchronization cost should be controlled independently by the network budget. Recent work reduces synchronization traffic by losslessly encoding differences between consecutive policy snapshots. SparseRL-Sync transmits changed values and their indices ( Hu et al., 2026 ) , while ARC exploits unchanged values and bit-level redundancy ( Fireworks AI, 2026 ) . These methods preserve the BF16 snapshots exactly and can achieve substantial savings when rounding leaves many weights unchanged. Their payloads, however, depend on the changes that must be preserved and the redundancy available to the codec. Consequently, lossless encoding alone does not guarantee a prescribed per-update communication budget.

We therefore ask whether synchronization must operate on parameter changes at all. For a gradient-driven optimizer with reproducible transitions, the next state is determined by the current parameters, optimizer state, gradient and update configuration. Distributed data-parallel training uses this principle to keep replicas synchronized through shared gradients and local optimizer updates ( Li et al., 2020 ) . A rollout worker can likewise reconstruct the learner’s update from the same gradient by maintaining replicated parameters and optimizer state under matched execution. This moves compression before the optimizer step, allowing established gradient-compression methods ( Lin et al., 2018 ; Vogels et al., 2019 ) to exploit gradient structure before optimizer transformations reshape the update (§ 3.3 ). Building on this insight, we introduce HiLo ( Hi gh-rank in training, Lo w-rank on the wire), a framework for communication-efficient LoRA synchronization in distributed on-policy post-training. HiLo replaces parameter transmission with compressed gradient dissemination and local optimizer replay, reducing synchronization traffic without lowering the training rank. We further develop Spar (Spectral Packing with Adaptive Ranks), a budget-aware gradient compressor tailored to LoRA that serves as a backend for HiLo. Together, HiLo and Spar alleviate the synchronization bottleneck, allowing distributed rollout to scale more effectively over bandwidth-constrained networks. Our main contributions are as follows.

• We formalize HiLo as a compressor-agnostic optimizer-replay protocol and establish conditions for matching learner and worker parameters and optimizer states at the same policy version. This enables different gradient-compression backends to plug into the same synchronization protocol while preserving same-version consistency. • We design Spar to compress LoRA-factor gradients using spectral truncation via small Gram-matrix eigendecompositions, global rank allocation under a byte budget, and error feedback. The resulting allocation prioritizes gradient directions with the highest spectral value per communicated byte. • We evaluate HiLo on two reasoning tasks and test robustness across four optimizers. With Spar, HiLo maintains accuracy close to full synchronization at 1.6% of the adapter bytes and achieves up to 2.2 × 2.2\times end-to-end speedup on bandwidth-limited links. On-policy post-training improves a student policy π 𝜽 \pi_{\bm{\theta}} by learning from responses y ∼ π 𝜽 ( ⋅ ∣ x ) y\sim\pi_{\bm{\theta}}(\cdot\mid x) sampled from its own evolving distribution. Two representative approaches are reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) and on-policy distillation (OPD). In RLVR, a verifier evaluates responses using task-specific correctness signals, and policy-gradient algorithms such as GRPO optimize the student using reward-derived advantages ( Shao et al., 2024 ) . In OPD, a teacher provides token-level supervision along student-generated trajectories, typically through a divergence-based distillation objective ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ) . The two signals can also be combined in a single objective. Reinforcement-aware distillation (RLAD) ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) keeps a reward-driven PPO-style update but anchors its importance ratio partly to the teacher, so the teacher shapes the update without a separate KL term. Their supervision differs, but all of them learn from an evolving student policy.

In actor–learner architectures, rollout workers generate trajectories using local policy copies, while a learner computes gradients and updates parameters ( Sheng et al., 2025 ) . Trajectories flow from workers to the learner, and after every update the new policy must flow back to every worker. Synchronous execution places this transfer on the critical path and blocks rollout generation until it completes, whereas asynchronous execution overlaps communication with computation at the cost of potentially stale policies. Decentralized systems take the asynchronous route and bound the lag explicitly. INTELLECT-2 lets workers generate with a policy a few updates old while checkpoints propagate through relay servers ( Prime Intellect Team et al., 2025 ) , and ECHO-2 caps staleness while pipelining the broadcast among peers ( Song et al., 2026 ) . Both change how and when the weights arrive, but every worker still receives the full policy. Many on-policy objectives, such as distillation, need samples from the current student and tolerate little lag. For instance, synchronizing the full policy only every few updates can noticeably degrade the student once the lag grows (Appendix C.2 ). We study this learner-to-worker path.

Let S S be the bytes the learner sends per update and N N the number of workers. Under unicast over a learner uplink of bandwidth B B , each update spends about N ​ S / B NS/B seconds in transfer, and relay or pipelined broadcast ( Prime Intellect Team et al., 2025 ; Song et al., 2026 ) only moves this bottleneck to each worker’s downlink. For LoRA, S S grows linearly with the training rank r r . The rank-64 adapter of Qwen3-1.7B is 139.5 MB in BF16, and at 62.5 Mbps per worker its transfer alone exceeds the 15 s of computation per update (§ 4.3 ). Existing remedies each give something up. Lowering r r caps what the adapter can learn, and the rank a workload needs is not known in advance ( Schulman and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025 ; Biderman et al., 2024 ) . Lossless delta codecs ( Fireworks AI, 2026 ; Hu et al., 2026 ) rely on the sparsity of full-parameter updates, whereas a LoRA update is dense. Lossy compression of the adapter or of its change truncates the optimizer’s output, which is generically full rank in factor space, and if only the workers adopt the truncated weights, they sample from a policy the learner never held. This same-version discrepancy, 𝜽 v ( i ) ≠ 𝜽 v \bm{\theta}^{(i)}_{v}\neq\bm{\theta}_{v} for worker i i at version v v , is distinct from temporal staleness, the lag between v v and the learner’s current version. We therefore seek a message whose size is set by a byte budget rather than by r r , that learner and workers decode to the same state, and that applies to any gradient-driven optimizer. A worker that holds the parameters and optimizer state needs only the gradient, the one input that compresses well, so HiLo sends it and leaves staleness to the schedule.

We introduce HiLo , a communication-efficient LoRA synchronization framework that replaces parameter transmission with compressed gradient dissemination and local optimizer replay. As illustrated in Figure 1 , the learner compresses aggregated LoRA-factor gradients with error feedback, while both the learner and rollout workers apply the same decoded gradients through locally maintained optimizer states. HiLo supports different gradient compressors. We further develop Spar , a LoRA-specific backend that combines Gram-matrix-based low-rank approximation with budget-aware rank allocation across factors, so that synchronization traffic no longer depends on the training rank.

chunks.section: 3.3 Why the Gradient Rather than the Update
chunks.text: Compressing after the optimizer, as the parameter-side methods of § 2.3 do (the Delta baseline of § 4.1 and LoGRA), truncates a different object. Under SGD the update is a multiple of the gradient and both truncations discard the same energy, but momentum raises the update’s rank by the communication rank at every step, and AdamW’s coordinatewise normalization replaces the gradient’s spectrum with that of its second-moment statistics, so a rank-one gradient stream generically yields a full-rank update in factor space (Appendix A ). In a synthetic AdamW replay, a rank-one truncation keeps all of the gradient but only 20–40% of the update (Table 4 ).

Replay costs worker memory and computation. For | 𝜽 | |\bm{\theta}| trainable LoRA entries, FP32 AdamW moments cost 8 ​ | 𝜽 | 8|\bm{\theta}| bytes and FP32 Muon momentum 4 ​ | 𝜽 | 4|\bm{\theta}| , plus master parameters and buffers where used, and replay adds the optimizer’s local update cost, including orthogonalization for Muon. For a factor of shape a × b a\times b decoded at rank k k , reconstruction costs O ⁡ ( a ​ b ​ k ) O(abk) operations. Encoder timings are in § 4.3 and the cost model in Appendix E.4 .

Delta uses error feedback to compress post-optimizer changes at the same payload; the learner adopts the compressed weights, so workers keep no optimizer state. In this section, we evaluate HiLo on two reasoning tasks. § 4.1 describes the setup and verifies that replay reproduces the learner’s state, § 4.2 compares learning quality against full synchronization and the baselines at matched payloads, and § 4.3 measures payload, overhead and end-to-end step time with live worker replay.

We evaluate on two reasoning tasks from Reasoning Gym ( Stojanovski et al., 2025 ) that differ in their training signal. Knights and Knaves (KK) ( Xie et al., 2024 ) asks which of six inhabitants tell the truth and which lie, given their statements. We train it with pure OPD, minimizing the sampled-token reverse KL divergence to a Qwen3-8B teacher ( Qwen Team, 2025 ) . Countdown-4 ( Gandhi et al., 2024 ) asks for an arithmetic expression over four given numbers that reaches a target value. We train it with the RLAD objective ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) , combining a verifiable task reward with the log-probabilities of the same teacher (Appendices C.2 and D.3 ). The main KK student is Qwen3-1.7B-Base with a rank-64 LoRA adapter, and the Countdown-4 student is Qwen3-0.6B-Base with a rank-64 LoRA adapter. All adapters use the rank-stabilized scale s = α / r s=\alpha/\sqrt{r} for LoRA ( Kalajdzievski, 2023 ) . For both tasks, we report accuracy on 1,000 held-out problems disjoint from the training set, with a 2,048-token generation cap.

Full Sync trains a rank-64 adapter and ships it in full after every update, the uncompressed reference. Low-rank LoRA ( r = k r{=}k ) lowers the training rank to k k and fully synchronizes the adapter. Delta keeps rank 64 and instead compresses the post-optimizer parameter change. The learner adds its carried error, ships the rank- k k truncation and adopts the truncated weights itself, so workers need no optimizer state. HiLo keeps rank 64 and compresses only the gradient. Besides our Spar backend, we instantiate it with PowerSGD ( Vogels et al., 2019 ) using one warm-started power iteration and with Top- k k ( Lin et al., 2018 ) sending a BF16 value and an int32 index per entry. All HiLo variants apply error feedback ( Karimireddy et al., 2019 ) before the optimizer and are matched to the analytical rank- k k payload ℬ k \mathcal{B}_{k} of Equation 4 , so they differ only in the backend (Appendix D.1 ).

For Spar, the low-rank factors are transmitted in BF16 ( q = 2 q=2 bytes per scalar), with error feedback computed against the decoded gradients. Unless stated otherwise, all methods use AdamW with a learning rate of 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} with linear decay, and every configuration is run with three seeds. Each KK update samples 16 prompts × \times 8 rollouts, and KK training runs for 300 updates. Each Countdown-4 update samples 64 prompts × \times 8 rollouts, keeps the 32 groups with non-constant reward, and the schedule spans 200 updates after a 10-step warmup. KK actors serve the LoRA adapter unmerged through vLLM’s LoRA kernels ( Kwon et al., 2023 ) , whereas Countdown-4 actors serve merged BF16 weights and may generate one update behind the learner. In every compressed method the learner itself follows the compressed trajectory, so actors never sample from parameters the learner does not hold. For the HiLo variants, actors obtain their parameters through a replay simulator that applies each decoded gradient to a replicated optimizer state, and its output matches the learner bitwise in every run we checked; for Delta they receive the truncated weights (Appendix D.1 ). All runs use NVIDIA GH200 GPUs. At the end of training, we evaluate four samples per problem at temperature 1.0 and report pass@4 and mean@4.

Before comparing methods, we verify the same-version consistency of optimizer replay (§ 3.1 ). A Qwen3-0.6B-Base learner with rank-32 LoRA and Spar at rank 1 consumes exactly the decoded BF16 gradient and records the initial LoRA parameters and every shipped factor. A separate process on another GH200 GPU replays AdamW from these inputs alone. Over 60 KK updates, all 392 LoRA tensors match the learner bitwise at every tenth update (maximum absolute difference 0). Both processes share the GPU type and software stack, so heterogeneous execution remains unverified (Appendix E.1 ).

Table 1 shows that keeping the training rank and compressing only the gradient preserves learning quality, with the largest benefit from Spar at the tightest budgets. On KK at rank 1 (1.6% of the bytes), HiLo + Spar reaches 81.6% pass@4 against 83.2% for Full Sync, ahead of HiLo + PowerSGD (78.8%), Low-rank LoRA (78.0%) and HiLo + Top- k k (76.6%), and it matches Full Sync at rank 2. Delta trails it by 6.2 points at rank 1, because the gradient’s rank- k k tail is set by the data whereas the AdamW update’s is set by the second-moment statistics (§ 3.3 ). On Countdown-4 under RLAD, Spar reaches 63.7% at rank 1 against 64.0% for Full Sync, ahead of PowerSGD and Low-rank LoRA in every seed, and its global budget still reaches 62.5% at 0.78% of the bytes. Low-rank LoRA trails HiLo + Spar at the smallest ranks on both tasks, which supports keeping the training rank. As the budget grows the backends converge, so the backend matters most when bandwidth is scarce. With three seeds, the margin over PowerSGD at a single rank is within about two standard deviations, and the evidence is the consistent trend across ranks and tasks.

Because HiLo replays whatever transition the optimizer defines, we repeat the Countdown-4 comparison at rank 1 under AdamW, Muon ( Jordan, 2024 ) , Lion ( Chen et al., 2023 ) and SGD with momentum, with five seeds per arm and the learning rate tuned for Full Sync per optimizer (Appendix C.2 ). Figure 3 shows that HiLo + Spar is the only compressed method that stays within 3 pass@4 points of Full Sync under all four optimizers. PowerSGD drops to 55.5% under Muon, Top- k k drops to 43.0% under Lion, and Low-rank LoRA trails Spar under every optimizer. Delta is the least robust, collapsing in all five Muon seeds and in one of five AdamW seeds, whereas no HiLo + Spar run collapses. Delta’s ordering across optimizers follows § 3.3 . Momentum raises the update’s rank only additively, AdamW makes it generically full, and Muon’s orthogonalization also flattens its spectrum, which makes truncation least effective. Delta’s parity with HiLo + Spar under Lion is not predicted by this rank argument (Appendix A.3 ).

Figure 4: Per-update communication payload and pass@4 on Countdown-4. HiLo + Spar ( k = 1 k=1 ) sends 62 × \times fewer bytes than full adapter synchronization and 17 × \times fewer than the strongest lossless delta codec, at comparable accuracy. Payload ratios are relative to HiLo; the lossless methods reproduce Full Sync exactly and share its accuracy.

Deployed systems shrink the policy payload by encoding the change between consecutive weight versions without loss ( Fireworks AI, 2026 ; Hu et al., 2026 ) . On the rank-64 Countdown-4 adapter (Figure 4 ), about 61% of the BF16 elements change between consecutive updates, so SparseRL-Sync, which sends the changed values and their indices, saves only 16% over Full Sync. ARCv2 and ARCv3 reduce the payload to 27.1 and 22.9 MB, whereas HiLo + Spar at k = 1 k{=}1 sends 1.3 MB, 17 × \times less, at a cost of 0.3 pass@4 points. ARCv3 also takes 12–14 s to encode each update.

On one GH200, the Spar encoder takes 25–27 ms per update for the 392 factor gradients of the rank-64 Qwen3-1.7B adapter, against 35–41 ms for one-iteration PowerSGD, 22–24 ms for Top- k k and about 550 ms for exact batched SVD, and a worker rebuilds the gradient in 13–19 ms. Spar, PowerSGD and Top- k k thus stay below 0.5% of a 15 s lockstep update (Appendix E.4 ). The end-to-end runs below used the slower torch.linalg.eigh path, about 0.27 s more per update (Appendix E.3 ).

We run the Qwen3-1.7B KK recipe with one learner GPU and eight workers on three GH200 nodes (Table 3 ). Each worker scores its own rollouts with the Qwen3-8B teacher, and under HiLo it receives the BF16 rank-1 gradient factors and replays AdamW live. Links are TCP-paced to a fixed bandwidth per worker, and 62.5 and 125 Mbps per worker correspond to unicast learner uplinks of 0.5 and 1 Gbps, the same order as the WAN regimes of ECHO-2 ( Song et al., 2026 ) . We presented HiLo, which synchronizes LoRA policies in distributed on-policy post-training by sending compressed gradients and letting rollout workers replay the optimizer locally, and Spar, a budget-aware backend that decouples training rank from communication rank. HiLo stays close to full synchronization at 1.6% of the adapter bytes and speeds up each update by up to 2.2 × 2.2\times on bandwidth-limited links. More broadly, by decoupling what the learner trains from what it must ship, HiLo makes distributed rollout practical in communication-constrained settings, from geographically distributed clusters to heterogeneous compute shared over wide-area networks, without sacrificing adapter capacity.

The consistency guarantee is objective-independent, but the effect of gradient compression on learning is not, and we measure it only for OPD and RLAD. Pure GRPO gradient-synchronization results are still needed to validate quality beyond these settings.

Worker state memory depends on the optimizer (§ 3.3 ). For the current rank-64 1.7B configuration ( | 𝜽 | = 69,730,304 |\bm{\theta}|=69{,}730{,}304 ), the FP32 AdamW moments alone occupy approximately 558 MB per worker and add to startup and recovery traffic. Exact reconstruction also requires matching optimizer versions, update ordering and numerical kernels; heterogeneous execution, numerical quantization, dropped messages and restarts require empirical validation. State equality does not establish identical sampled trajectories across different inference kernels. The end-to-end links are paced inside one cluster, so wide-area latency, jitter and loss are not modeled.

PowerSGD ( Vogels et al., 2019 ) and Deep Gradient Compression ( Lin et al., 2018 ) compress gradient communication in data-parallel training, and error feedback compensates omitted directions over time ( Seide et al., 2014 ; Karimireddy et al., 2019 ) . 1-bit Adam ( Tang et al., 2021 ) combines communication compression with adaptive optimization through a distinct training recipe, and GaLore ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) gives conditions under which dense weight gradients become low-rank. HiLo does not introduce gradient compression itself. It moves the compressor to a different interface, after aggregation on the learner and before one-to-many dissemination to inference-only workers, where a global byte budget and exact short-side decompositions become practical.

INTELLECT-2 relays weights through Shardcast ( Prime Intellect Team et al., 2025 ) , and ECHO-2 combines bounded staleness, overlap of communication with computation and pipelined peer-to-peer broadcast ( Song et al., 2026 ) . These mechanisms change how a payload travels rather than what it contains, so HiLo’s gradient messages could be relayed in the same way. Lossless weight-delta codecs shrink the payload itself. Fireworks AI reconstructs the trainer’s weights bit for bit from compressed BF16 deltas ( Fireworks AI, 2026 ) , and SparseRL-Sync sends only the changed elements of full-parameter updates ( Hu et al., 2026 ) . Both rely on most weights staying unchanged between versions. A LoRA update is dense in parameter space, so these codecs save little on adapters (§ 4.3 ), whereas its factor gradients remain compressible. IMPALA ( Espeholt et al., 2018 ) separates actors from learners with off-policy correction, LoRA serving systems ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Sheng et al., 2024 ) make adapter installation cheap, and infrequent synchronization ( Douillard et al., 2023 ) trades communication for staleness, which on our Countdown-4 runs costs far more accuracy than gradient compression at the same bytes (Appendix C.2 ). None of them reduces the size of each repeated adapter transfer.

Concurrent with this work, LoGRA ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) accumulates random low-rank sketches of the gradients of selected weight matrices during backpropagation and synchronizes rollout engines with the optimizer-adjusted low-rank update. It targets training memory in full-weight RL, whereas HiLo targets learner-to-worker bandwidth for an existing high-rank LoRA adapter. LoGRA runs the optimizer only on the trainer, so rollout engines receive a parameter update of at most the sketch rank, as in our Delta baseline. In HiLo, workers replay the full optimizer transition from the decoded gradient, so an adaptive optimizer such as AdamW can still produce a full-rank update in factor space (Appendix A ). To see whether LoGRA’s update carries over to LoRA factors, we apply a LoGRA-style update to the rank-64 Countdown-4 adapter at the Spar rank-1 payload (Table 5 ). Each step sketches every factor gradient along its long side with a fresh seeded random sign matrix, keeps RowAdam state and applies the low-rank update. We do not use LoGRA’s predicted-KL step control and sweep the learning rate instead, so this is not a full reproduction of LoGRA. The best setting reaches 51.6% pass@4 against 64.1% for Spar, and larger learning rates collapse. A random sketch of a factor’s long side keeps about 1.6% of the gradient energy per update here, whereas Spar ships the dominant directions exactly and keeps 13.8%. Random sketches can amortize over many steps in full-weight training, but on a LoRA factor the same payload carries far less signal per update.

Each optimizer is replayed with its own replicated state and numerical implementation, and the online bitwise checks of the replay simulator cover all four.

PowerSGD and Top- k k run as alternative HiLo backends with the same error feedback and payload as Spar, so they serve both as competitors and as instances of the framework. Compressor state includes the error-feedback residual, and PowerSGD also keeps its warm start. PowerSGD uses one warm-started power iteration, since additional iterations add computation without reducing the payload. Exact truncation with k k directions per factor (“Exact, k k per factor” in Tables 2 and 6 ) is Spar without the global budget. Fixed ranks are a baseline configuration choice, and adaptive allocation could also be applied to PowerSGD. Low-rank LoRA ( r = k r{=}k ) instead trains a rank- k k adapter and synchronizes it in full. Delta keeps rank 64, runs the optimizer only on the learner, adds the carried error to each factor’s parameter change, truncates the result to rank k k at the same payload and adopts the truncated parameters itself, so workers need no optimizer state. Delta supports integer ranks only. In the learning-quality runs, every compressed method makes the learner follow the compressed trajectory. Actors in the HiLo variants obtain their parameters through a replay simulator that decodes each shipped gradient and applies it to a replicated optimizer state, and actors under Delta receive the truncated parameters. These runs therefore isolate how each backend affects learning, and live worker replay is measured separately with Spar (§ 4.3 ). The simulator output is compared bitwise with the learner online in a subset of runs.

Each KK puzzle has six inhabitants, including synonymous truth-teller and liar role pairs, and the scorer requires the final answer block to match the entire oracle assignment. The student is trained with sampled-token reverse-KL OPD to a Qwen3-8B teacher, using AdamW and 16 prompts × \times 8 rollouts per update. Actors and evaluation serve the LoRA adapter unmerged through vLLM’s LoRA kernels ( Kwon et al., 2023 ) . Evaluation uses 1,000 questions with no overlap with the training pool and a 2,048-token cap. Checkpoint horizons alter the learning-rate schedule and are not interchangeable. Low-rank LoRA and Top- k k at ranks 1 and 2 saved no update-300 checkpoint in their original runs, so we retrained them with the same recipe and seeds for Table 1 .

A replay implementation must make the learner consume the same quantized, decoded gradient as workers. Even identical factors can produce slightly different decoded matrices across GPU architectures or GEMM implementations. Matching parameter/state dtypes, tensor ordering, optimizer implementation and update configuration is therefore required for bitwise equality. For AdamW this includes bias correction and fused/foreach execution; for Muon it includes orthogonalization coefficients, iteration count, precision and GEMM execution. Randomized transitions also require matching random draws or counter-based seeds. A heterogeneous implementation must instead measure deviations rather than assume equality.

The learner (Qwen3-0.6B-Base, rank-32 LoRA, budgeted Gram compression at budget 1, two-GPU data parallel) rounds every shipped gradient factor to BF16 and consumes exactly the decoded gradient, as same-version consistency requires (§ 3.1 ). It records the initial LoRA parameters and each step’s BF16 factors. A separate process on a different GPU reads only these inputs, rebuilds each factor gradient with the learner’s batched reconstruction, and runs AdamW with the same hyperparameters and learning-rate schedule. Parameters are compared at every tenth update over 60 updates of KK distillation, and replaying the 60 updates takes 26 s including loading. Both sides use GH200 GPUs and the same software stack; heterogeneous hardware would require measuring, rather than assuming, equality.

Each message identifies its optimizer epoch, predecessor and target versions, tensor layout, factor ranks and dtypes, and shared configuration ξ t \xi_{t} , including scheduler index and implementation identity. Replacing a backlog with only the latest gradient is generally invalid for a stateful optimizer. Updates may be aggregated only when equivalence is established for the chosen transition. Recovery requires a retained update log or a snapshot containing both parameters and optimizer state; an adapter-only restart cannot recover omitted historical state.
